 No Democrat has won a Texas Senate race since 1988
Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow polling edge
Small-dollar donations face Musk-backed Republican money
Campaign spending sets records in a "seismic" contest
 International | Published 2026.11.04. 06:07:05 | By Park Min-ju mj@sedaily.com | Summary | Save A A A Supporters of the U.S. Democratic Party hold signs reading "Take back Texas" at the final campaign rally for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at Stubb's Waller Creek Amphitheater in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 2 local time. Reuters-Yonhap "The last time a Democrat won a statewide race in Texas, James Talarico was in kindergarten."
 That line from the Texas Tribune, a local news outlet, captures how long Republicans have gone unbeaten in Texas — more than three decades. The last Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race in the state did so in 1988, and the last Democratic governor was elected in 1990. Measured by statewide offices such as attorney general, Democrats last produced a winner in 1994. Talarico, born in 1989, was only 5 years old at the time.
 Yet for all its reputation as Republican heartland, Texas is showing signs of an upset in this year's midterm elections. Polls have put Talarico ahead of Republican candidate Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race, and forecasters increasingly see a close contest in the governor's race as well.
 The Senate fight: a 37-year-old former teacher vs. a 64-year-old attorney general
 James Talarico, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas. AP-Yonhap Ken Paxton, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas. EPA-Yonhap Talarico led Paxton in six of 10 polls, or 60%, according to RealClearPolling, a platform that aggregates election surveys, as of the 2nd local time. The widest margin came in a New York Times/Siena survey, which showed Talarico 7 percentage points ahead of Paxton. Three polls showed the two tied, while only one — Quantus Insights — projected a Paxton win, and even there the gap between the candidates was just 1 percentage point.
 The two have also drawn attention for their wide age gap. Talarico, 37, trained as a seminary student and taught briefly before entering politics with his election to the Texas House. Paxton, 64, has served as Texas attorney general since 2015 and is a seasoned politician who had already sat in the Texas Senate before taking the attorney general's office.
 Paxton's scandals are cited as the reason Talarico holds a narrow lead. Incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn attacked Paxton fiercely during the primary over allegations including an extramarital affair, a jump in his personal wealth and bribery, but Paxton won with President Donald Trump's backing, leaving Republican voters divided.
 Reuters pointed in particular to the affair as a source of unease among conservative women voters in Texas. Angela Paxton, his wife and a sitting member of the Texas Senate, filed for divorce last year citing adultery, and the episode has raised doubts among women voters, according to the report. Talarico, for his part, has drawn criticism from conservatives after videos resurfaced in which he defended transgender rights and abortion.
 Texas hosts the most expensive race in the U.S.
 Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX. Reuters-Yonhap The Texas Senate contest is also the most expensive Senate race in the country. Talarico said he raised $64 million in the third quarter of this year, the largest sum ever raised by a U.S. Senate candidate in a single quarter. Small donors giving less than $100 accounted for 97% of his third-quarter contributions.
 Republicans are matching that with heavy political money of their own, backed by a formidable patron: Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla. Musk is unusual among Big Tech CEOs in living in Texas rather than California. National Republican groups have poured $272 million into the race, most of it reportedly from Musk.
 The Texas Tribune reported that since early September, when Republican money began flowing, Talarico has faced $182 million worth of negative advertising from outside groups tied to Senate Republican leadership. As of the 29th of last month, Paxton's supporters had spent $265.6 million on advertising and Talarico's $119.9 million.
 Latino voters hold another key
 Latino voters, credited as a driving force behind Trump's presidential victory, are also turning away, analysts say. Trump won about 55% of Hispanic voters in the 2024 presidential election. But those voters are now worried about a weakening economy and the Trump administration's hard-line immigration policy, CBS reported.
 As of early last month, Trump's approval rating among Latino voters stood at just 24%, and among those who voted for him in the presidential election, 57% approved of his handling of the job — down sharply from 93% in February of last year. Latino voters make up more than 30% of the Texas electorate.
 The race between Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has held the office for 12 years, and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa is also drawing interest. Abbott leads Hinojosa by an average of 3 percentage points in polls, but Democrats see hope in the narrowed margin. Expectations that Republicans will still make gains persist. A University of Texas poll found that about 49% of Texas voters identify with or lean Republican, against roughly 40% for Democrats.
 James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said this is the most competitive contest between the two parties since Republicans took control. "If Talarico or Hinojosa wins, it will mark a political earthquake," he said.
